title: North America: Home, Country & Improvised Ferments
attribution: The ferments North Americans make at home rather than buy: country fruit and berry wines put up in a crock, wine from the native grapes that grow where vinifera will not, foraged flower wines, and — documented to warn rather than to instruct — the improvised ferments of the prison system. Sourced to land-grant cooperative extension bulletins (UGA, NC State, Illinois) and, for pruno, public-health reporting. Where extension publishes a target the figures are theirs; where a drink is pure folk tradition no numbers are asserted.

styles.name: Pruno (Prison Wine)
styles.impression: An improvised alcoholic drink fermented in secret from whatever sugar and fruit is at hand — the archetypal 'anything ferments' beverage, and a genuine public-health hazard, not a novelty.
styles.comments: DANGER — this is a warning entry, not a recipe. Pruno has caused documented outbreaks of botulism, a paralytic and potentially fatal poisoning: the CDC reported eight hospitalisations in a single 2013 outbreak traced to a batch that included a baked potato, a classic source of Clostridium botulinum spores. It carries no numeric style targets here and never will, because encouraging precision would be encouraging the drink. It is catalogued so the record is honest about what people ferment, and so anyone who finds it here reads the danger first.
styles.history: A folk ferment of the North American prison system, made covertly because alcohol is prohibited inside. Improvised from commissary and kitchen ingredients and hidden while it works.
styles.comparison: Related in spirit to every other improvised folk ferment in this section — the difference is that pruno's typical ingredients and conditions make botulism a real and repeatedly documented risk.
styles.tags: north-america, improvised, prison, folk-ferment, hazard, botulism-risk, warning, no-recipe

styles.name: Blackberry Wine
styles.impression: A dark, brambly country wine from the most-made wild berry in the American home cellar — deeply coloured, tart, and traditionally sweetened back.
styles.comments: UGA Extension Circular 717 sets the country-wine method: crush the fruit, sterilise with sulphite, adjust acid, tannin and sugar, pitch an activated yeast, run a 3–7 day primary on the pulp, strain, then a sealed secondary with periodic racking, about a month in all at 60–70 °F. A must brought to 22% sugar targets roughly 11% ABV.
styles.history: Home fruit wine is the oldest continuous winemaking tradition in North America — made wherever the fruit grew and grapes did not, from surplus, windfall and foraged crops, in crocks and carboys rather than a winery.
styles.ingredients: Fruit, water, sugar to bring the must to strength, acid and tannin adjustment as the fruit requires, campden or potassium metabisulphite, and yeast. UGA C717 recommends a true wine yeast such as Montrachet No. 522 and accepts baker's yeast as an alternative — the low-equipment tradition in a sentence.
styles.comparison: Fermented to full strength as a wine, unlike cider or perry, which ferment their fruit's own sugar at its natural gravity.

styles.name: Muscadine Wine
styles.impression: Wine from Vitis rotundifolia, the grape of the American South — thick-skinned, musky, high in acid and low in fermentable sugar, so the must is corrected before it will make wine.
styles.comments: UGA Extension Circular 717 sets the country-wine method: crush the fruit, sterilise with sulphite, adjust acid, tannin and sugar, pitch an activated yeast, run a 3–7 day primary on the pulp, strain, then a sealed secondary with periodic racking, about a month in all at 60–70 °F. A must brought to 22% sugar targets roughly 11% ABV. Named cultivars include Hunt, Cowart, Carlos and Scuppernong.
styles.history: Muscadine has been cultivated for more than 400 years. Native Americans dried the grapes long before European settlement, and Spanish settlements in Florida were making muscadine wine in quantity as early as 1565 — the oldest documented winemaking in what is now the United States.
styles.ingredients: Muscadine grapes, sugar, acid correction, campden, wine yeast. UGA notes the muscadine is one of the few fruits carrying all the nutrients yeast needs, and recommends a true wine yeast such as Montrachet No. 522.
styles.comparison: Nothing like a vinifera wine: the musky aroma and slipskin texture are the point, not a fault.
styles.tags: north-america, muscadine, native-grape, southern, country-wine, extension-sourced

styles.name: Scuppernong (Bronze Muscadine) Wine
styles.impression: The bronze-skinned muscadine, and the source of the South's most misused wine name.
styles.comments: Carries no separate targets from muscadine wine; it is a cultivar distinction, recorded because the name is so widely applied to bronze muscadines generally that the actual variety is usually lost.
styles.history: The first recognised muscadine cultivar was found in North Carolina before 1760, known first as the 'Big White Grape' and later named Scuppernong. NC State Extension is explicit that the name became generic for all bronze muscadines and that this is incorrect nomenclature — Scuppernong is one cultivar among many.
styles.ingredients: Bronze muscadine grapes, otherwise as for muscadine wine.
styles.comparison: A colour-and-cultivar distinction within muscadine, not a separate style of winemaking.
styles.tags: north-america, scuppernong, muscadine, bronze, nomenclature, extension-sourced

styles.name: Concord & Fox Grape Wine
styles.impression: Wine from Vitis labrusca and its hybrids — the grape of the Northeast, unmistakably foxy, usually finished sweet because it is punishing when dry.
styles.comments: Made by the same country-wine method; the characteristic methyl-anthranilate 'foxy' aroma is intrinsic to the species, not a fermentation fault.
styles.history: The labrusca grape carried American home winemaking north of the muscadine belt, where its cold-hardiness and disease resistance let it grow when European vines would not.
styles.ingredients: Concord or other labrusca grapes, sugar and acid correction, campden, wine yeast.
styles.comparison: Shares with muscadine the fact of being a native American species wine rather than a vinifera one; the aromatics are entirely different.
styles.tags: north-america, concord, labrusca, foxy, native-grape, country-wine

styles.name: Dandelion Wine
styles.impression: The archetypal foraged flower wine: petals steeped to make the base, then sugared and fermented — a wine made from a lawn weed and a bag of sugar, and the purest expression of the no-equipment tradition.
styles.comments: No numeric targets are given here. Dandelion wine is a folk recipe with no published extension specification, and inventing a gravity or ABV for it would be pretending to a precision the tradition does not have.
styles.history: Dandelions are not native to North America. Europeans brought them over in the 1600s deliberately, as an edible and medicinal crop rather than a weed; the plant has been in continuous use as food and medicine for at least a thousand years. The wine travelled with it.
styles.ingredients: Dandelion petals (the green parts are bitter and are picked out), sugar, water, citrus for acid, and yeast — historically whatever was in the kitchen.
styles.comparison: Structurally a sugar wine flavoured by infusion, closer to a flower mead without the honey than to a fruit wine.
styles.tags: north-america, dandelion, foraged, flower-wine, folk-recipe, no-figures

styles.name: Garden & Root Wines
styles.impression: Wines from whatever the garden produced too much of — rhubarb, elderberry, tomato, parsnip, beet. Made because the crop would otherwise be wasted, not because anyone set out to make that wine.
styles.comments: These follow the country-wine method but carry no published targets of their own; extension bulletins do not specify them, so no gravity or ABV is asserted here.
styles.history: A thrift tradition of the American farmhouse and the Plain communities, where a glut of a crop and a stone crock were reason enough. The same logic that produced country fruit wine, applied to whatever was left.
styles.ingredients: The garden or foraged crop, sugar to bring it to wine strength, acid and tannin as needed, and yeast.
styles.comparison: Same method as the fruit wines above; the base is a vegetable, root or hedgerow crop rather than an orchard one.
styles.tags: north-america, rhubarb, elderberry, root-wine, garden-wine, thrift, folk-recipe, no-figures
